paper_title: 3D CoCa v3: Contrastive Learners with Scene Graphs for Urban Scene Understanding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Understanding large-scale 3D urban scenes requires representations that capture both multi-scale geometric structures and complex spatial relationships. However, existing 3D vision-language methods primarily emphasize global semantic alignment or object-level representations, leaving structured relational modeling underexplored within unified contrastive and generative frameworks. In this paper, we present 3D CoCa v3, a scene-graph-enhanced contrastive and generative framework for urban 3D scene understanding. Our framework features a Pyramid Vision Encoder for multi-scale geometric representation learning and a language-model-based decoder with question-guided caption retrieval and visual cross-attention. We further introduce MSG-based relational descriptions to enrich contrastive 3D-language alignment with structured spatial relationships. To support semantic and relational supervision, we construct City3D-9.6K, a multi-view urban vision-language dataset with aligned visual-geometric observations, scene captions, and scene graphs. Extensive experiments on City-3DQA demonstrate that 3D CoCa v3 achieves 88.35% and 64.79% overall top-1 accuracy on the sentence-wise and city-wise splits, surpassing 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points, respectively. Furthermore, 3D CoCa v3 achieves the best performance on GeoEval3D, demonstrating its effectiveness in urban spatial reasoning and geometric understanding. Code is available at https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/3DCoCav3.

sections.content: Understanding large-scale 3D urban scenes requires representations that capture both multi-scale geometric structures and complex spatial relationships. However, existing 3D vision-language methods primarily emphasize global semantic alignment or object-level representations, leaving structured relational modeling underexplored within unified contrastive and generative frameworks. In this paper, we present 3D CoCa v3, scene-graph-enhanced contrastive and generative framework for urban 3D scene understanding. To support semantic and relational supervision, we construct City3D-9.6K, multi-view urban visionlanguage dataset with aligned visual-geometric observations, scene captions, and scene graphs. Code: https: //github.com/AIGeeksGroup/3DCoCav3. 1. Introduction Understanding large-scale 3D urban scenes is essential for spatial intelligence, with applications in 3D scene captioning [18], spatial reasoning [13, 16], and embodied navigation [14, 15, 27]. Compared with indoor environments, urban scenes exhibit complex geometric structures, diverse object categories, and intricate spatial relationships across Figure 1. Comparison of 3D CoCa, 3D CoCa v2, and our 3D CoCa v3. Previous methods focus on indoor 3D scene understanding through contrastive learning, generative captioning, and testtime search. Our framework extends this paradigm to urban scenes with geometry-aware multi-view representations, MSG-based relational descriptions, and question-guided multimodal decoding. multiple scales. Understanding such environments requires not only recognizing individual objects but also capturing their spatial configurations and semantic relationships. Recent advances in vision-language learning have enabled models to associate 3D observations with natural-language descriptions, supporting tasks such as question answering, visual grounding, and scene captioning. These developments underscore the importance of learning 3D representations that capture both geometric structures and spatial relationships in complex urban environments. Existing 3D vision-language methods have evolved from task-specific understanding to unified representation learning and structured spatial reasoning. Early approaches, such as ScanQA [1], explored question answering over 3D scenes, while 3D-VLP [23] and 3D-VisTA [44] learned transferable representations through cross-modal alignment. Building upon contrastive and generative learning, 3D CoCa [17] jointly optimizes 3D-text alignment and caption generation, while 3D CoCa v2 [36] further enhances caption generalization through test-time search. Beyond semantic alignment, scene-graph-based methods [26, 42] incorporate explicit object relationships to facilitate strucTable 1. Comparison of urban 3D vision-language datasets. Extending 3D understanding to urban environments, City-3DQA [34] introduces cityscale question-answering benchmark and scene-graphenhanced reasoning framework, while 3DCity-LLM [8] explores coarse-to-fine representations for city-scale perception and understanding. Collectively, these advances establish important foundations for geometric representation learning, cross-modal alignment, and relational reasoning in 3D environments. Despite these advances, existing methods still face challenges in urban 3D scene understanding. Current 3D visionlanguage frameworks primarily emphasize global semantic alignment or object-level representations, making it difficult to preserve fine-grained geometric details while capturing large-scale spatial context. Meanwhile, although scene graphs provide explicit relational information, effectively integrating structured spatial relationships into joint contrastive and generative learning remains underexplored in complex urban environments. These limitations motivate unified 3D vision-language framework that jointly captures multi-scale geometric structures and spatial relationships through contrastive and generative representation learning. To this end, we propose 3D CoCa v3, unified contrastive and generative framework for urban 3D scene understanding. As illustrated in Fig. 1, our framework extends the 3D CoCa paradigm from indoor scenes to complex urban environments through geometry-aware representation learning and relational language supervision. Our framework features Pyramid Vision Encoder for multiscale geometric representation learning, coupled with CapPa-inspired architecture and larger language-modelbased decoder for scene captioning and question answering. We further develop MSG-based contrastive learning, which incorporates structured scene-graph relationships into 3D-language alignment to enrich relational representations. In addition, we construct City3D-9.6K, synthetic urban scene dataset with paired scene captions and scene graphs, providing complementary semantic and relational supervision. Through joint contrastive and generative learning, 3D CoCa v3 integrates multi-scale geometry, structured spatial relationships, and natural-language semantics into unified representation. Extensive experiments on City-3DQA demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, achieving 88.35% and 64.79% overall top-1 accuracy on the sentence-wise and city-wise splits, respectively, outperforming 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points. Furthermore, 3D CoCa v3 achieves the best performance on GeoEval3D, further demonstrating its capabilities in spatial reasoning and geometric understanding. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We present 3D CoCa v3, an enhanced contrastive and generative architecture featuring Pyramid Vision Encoder, CapPa-inspired captioning architecture, and larger language-model-based decoder for multi-scale geometric representation learning and urban 3D scene understanding. We develop MSG-based contrastive learning that incorporates structured scene-graph relationships into 3Dlanguage representation learning. We further introduce City3D-9.6K, synthetic urban dataset with paired scene captions and scene graphs to support semantic and relational supervision. Extensive experiments on City-3DQA and GeoEval3D demonstrate the effectiveness of 3D CoCa v3. Our method achieves 88.35% and 64.79% overall top-1 accuracy on the sentence-wise and city-wise splits of City3DQA, outperforming 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points, respectively. 2. Related Work 3D vision-language scene understanding. Early 3D vision-language methods, such as ScanQA [1], 3DVLP [23], and 3D-VisTA [44], established 3D question answering and cross-modal representation learning from point clouds. SceneVerse [20] expanded grounded 3D-language supervision, while UniScene3D [29] learned geometry-aware representations from multi-view colored point maps. Recent approaches further strengthen spatial representations through compact 3D proxies [21] and explicit 3D grounding [11]. Beyond indoor environments, City-3DQA [34] establishes question answering over urban point clouds, whereas GeoProg3D [40] supports compositional reasoning in city-scale 3D language fields. These settings demand representations that capture both large-scale geometry and inter-object relations. Scene graphs for spatial reasoning. Scene graphs organize objects and their semantic or spatial relationships into structured representations for compositional reasoning. Sg-CityU [34] incorporates scene graphs into urban Figure 2. Construction pipeline of City3D-9.6K. (a) Multi-view RGB images and point maps are rendered from urban point clouds, with corresponding view-level captions generated by Qwen. (b) Multi-view scene graphs (MSG) associate shared entities and spatial relationships across viewpoints, providing structured context for scene-level caption generation. question answering, while 3DGraphLLM [42] encodes relational structures as learnable inputs to language models. Beyond object-centric relationships, MSG [43] constructs topological scene graphs by associating place and object nodes across multiple viewpoints, while HSG [39] extends scene graph representations to hyperbolic space to capture hierarchical relationships. View-on-Graph [28] further explores selective graph-based reasoning for zero-shot 3D visual grounding. For cross-modal representation learning, CCL-3DSGG [5] aligns 3D scene graph features with image and text representations, while scene graph-guided pretraining [26] leverages structured relations for fine-grained 3D-language contrastive alignment. These advances highlight the potential of structured relational representations for geometry-aware vision-language understanding in complex 3D environments. Contrastive and generative 3D learning. CLIP [33] established large-scale contrastive vision-language pre-training, while CoCa [41] combined contrastive alignment with autoregressive captioning, and CapPa [38] explored parallel caption prediction. For 3D captioning, Scan2Cap [9] and Vote2Cap-DETR++ [6, 7] model object descriptions and surrounding context; TOD3Cap [22] extends dense captioning to outdoor scenes, and Curvature-Aware Captioning [12] models geometric and semantic hierarchies through geodesic attention. 3D CoCa [17] transfers joint contrastive and generative learning to point clouds, with 3D CoCa v2 [36] further introducing test-time search for caption selection. Building on this line of work, we study graph-aware contrastive representations together with scene-level caption supervision and caption-conditioned question answering for urban 3D understanding. 3. Dataset: City3D-9.6K Dataset construction. We introduce City3D-9.6K, multi-view 3D vision-language dataset built upon City3DQA [34]. The original benchmark comprises 193 urban point-cloud scenes with diverse geometric structures and spatial relationships. As illustrated in Fig. 2, we extend these scenes with multi-view visual observations and hierarchical language annotations. Specifically, we render 50 viewpoints for each scene, yielding 9,650 RGB images and their corresponding point maps. The paired RGB images and point maps provide aligned appearance and geometric information across different viewpoints, supporting geometry-aware visual representation learning. Hierarchical language annotations. We construct complementary language annotations at both view and scene levels. For each rendered RGB image, we employ Qwen to generate view-level caption describing visible objects, semantic attributes, and spatial configurations. To capture spatial relationships beyond individual viewpoints, we further construct Multi-view Scene Graphs (MSG) that associate shared entities and their relationships across views, as shown in Fig. 2(b). The resulting graph structures provide relational context for Qwen-based scene caption generation, capturing the semantic organization and spatial relationships of the urban environment. While view-level captions describe viewpoint-specific observations, MSG-based scene captions provide broader semantic context and structured relational information. These complementary annotations support contrastive representation learning and generative scene understanding. Dataset statistics and comparison. City3D-9.6K comFigure 3. Overview of 3D CoCa v3. The framework learns geometry-aware representations from multi-view RGB images and XYZ point maps through Scene-CLIP contrastive pre-training, complemented by MSG-derived relational descriptions. multimodal decoder subsequently integrates question-relevant scene captions and projected visual features into LoRA-adapted Qwen backbone for urban 3D question answering. prises 193 urban scenes, 9,650 rendered RGB images, 9,650 point maps, and 9,650 view-level captions, together with MSG annotations and scene-level captions. The original question-answer pairs from City-3DQA are retained without introducing additional QA annotations. Tab. 1 compares City3D-9.6K with representative urban 3D vision-language datasets. Our dataset extends the original urban point clouds with aligned multi-view visual, geometric, and linguistic observations, complemented by MSG-based scene-level descriptions. This hierarchical annotation scheme provides semantic and relational supervision for urban 3D scene understanding. at viewpoint v. During pre-training, geometry-aware vision encoder learns view-level representations through contrastive alignment with visual and linguistic supervision, while scene-level representations are obtained by aggregating features across viewpoints. Multi-view scene graphs (MSG) further provide structured relational information for generating scene descriptions. During decoding, questionrelevant captions are retrieved as textual context, and the pre-trained visual features are incorporated into Qwenbased language model through cross-attention. The resulting framework jointly exploits geometric observations and relational semantics for urban 3D scene understanding. 4. Method 4.1. Overview We present 3D CoCa v3, contrastive and generative framework for urban 3D scene understanding. As illustrated in Fig. 3, our framework consists of two stages: Scene-CLIP vision-language pre-training and multimodal language decoding. The former learns geometry-aware representations through multi-view cross-modal alignment, while the latter integrates visual features and question-relevant scene descriptions for spatial question answering. Decoder Question-guided caption retrieval. As illustrated in Fig. 3(b), the decoder exploits scene descriptions generated from MSG-based relational information. Given question and set of candidate scene captions Cs = {C1, . . . , CK}, we employ question-guided retrieval strategy to identify the most relevant description: = R(Q, Cs), (8) where denotes rule-based relevance function that considers entity correspondence, question type, and spatial relationships. The retrieval mechanism selects caption that provides supporting semantic or relational context. When no candidate satisfies the relevance criteria, the decoder uses the question without additional caption context. Visual-language decoding. We employ pretrained Qwenbased language model with parameter-efficient LoRA adaptation. The Scene-CLIP encoder is frozen during this stage, and its multi-view representations serve as visual memory. The retrieved caption is incorporated into the textual prompt together with the question: = Dϕ ([C ; Q]) , (9) where Dϕ denotes the LoRA-adapted language backbone and represents its textual hidden states. To integrate geometric information, the pre-trained view representations are projected into the language-model hidden space: = fproj ([z1, . . . , zV ]) , (10) where fproj is trainable visual feature projector. The textual representations attend to the projected visual features through gated cross-attention module: = CrossAttn(H, Z, Z), = + γ LN(A), (11) where γ is learnable fusion parameter. The fused hidden states are subsequently processed by the language-model head for answer prediction. Answer generation. The decoder predicts the answer autoregressively, conditioned on the question, retrieved scene caption, and visual representations. Given target answer = (a1, . . . , aT ), the training objective is LQA = (cid:88) t=1 log pΘ (at a<t, Q, , Z) , (12) where Θ denotes the trainable decoder parameters. The language-model backbone is adapted through LoRA, while the visual projector and cross-attention module are trained to establish geometric-language interactions. This design enables question answering to exploit complementary information from multi-view geometric observations and structured scene descriptions. 5. Experiments 5.1. Benchmark and Metrics City-3DQA. We evaluate 3D CoCa v3 on City-3DQA [34], city-scale 3D question-answering benchmark comprising approximately 450K question-answer pairs across 193 scenes from six cities. Following the official evaluation sentence-wise, where protocol, we consider two splits: question-answer pairs are divided into training, validation, and test sets across all six cities, and city-wise, where the splits contain disjoint cities. The benchmark includes single-hop questions involving direct scene understanding and multi-hop questions requiring compositional spatial reasoning. We report top-1 accuracy (Acc@1) and top-10 accuracy (Acc@10) for single-hop, multi-hop, and all questions. GeoEval3D. We further evaluate geographic spatial reasoning on GeoEval3D [40], city-scale benchmark introduced by GeoProg3D. GeoEval3D comprises 952 queries across five tasks: grounding (GRD), spatial reasoning (SPR), comparison (CMP), counting (CNT), and measurement (MES). Following the evaluation protocol, we report accuracy for SPR and CMP, mean absolute error (MAE) for CNT, and measurement errors in meters for height (MES-H) and distance (MES-D). We evaluate on both GoogleEarth and UrbanScene3D, with CMP and MES-H excluded from UrbanScene3D following the original benchmark. Higher accuracy and lower MAE indicate better performance. 5.2. Implementation Details We initialize the visual encoder from UniScene3D [29] and perform contrastive pre-training on the RGBpoint-map observations from City3D-9.6K. Each RGB image and its corresponding point map are processed at resolution of 224 224, with 32 views sampled per scene during pretraining. The encoder is optimized using AdamW with an initial learning rate of 1 104 and warmup cosine learning-rate schedule. For downstream question answering, we extract and cache visual representations from 50 rendered views per scene. We investigate CapPaand CoCa-style decoder architectures with pretrained Qwen-based language models. Our final decoder uses 2B-parameter Qwen backbone with LoRA adaptation and visual cross-attention. The languagemodel backbone is frozen, while the LoRA parameters, visual projection layers, and cross-attention module are optimized. We use LoRA rank of 16, an alpha of 32, and eight attention heads for visual cross-attention. The decoder is trained with AdamW using learning rate of 1 106 for 30 epochs. For caption-conditioned question answering, question-relevant scene description is selected from the candidate captions and incorporated into the language prompt, while the visual representations are provided through crossattention. 5.3. Main Results Comparison on City-3DQA. As shown in Tab. 2, 3D CoCa v3 achieves the highest overall Acc@1 under both evaluation splits. Under the sentence-wise split, our method achieves 88.35% overall Acc@1, outperforming 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 percentage points. Notably, single-hop and multi-hop accuracies improve from 82.20% and 55.89% to 97.73% and 80.97%, respectively, with substantial gain of 25.08 percentage points on multi-hop questions. Under the more challenging city-wise split, our method achieves 64.79% overall Acc@1, surpassing 3D CoCa v2 and SgCityU by 3.57 and 1.03 percentage points, respectively. It also achieves the highest multi-hop accuracy of 55.02%, outperforming 3D CoCa v2 by 5.06 percentage points. Although Acc@10 remains lower than that of several baselines, the consistent gains in overall and multi-hop Acc@1 highlight the effectiveness of our framework in top-ranked answer prediction and compositional spatial reasoning. Comparison on GeoEval3D. As shown in Tab. 3, 3D CoCa v3 achieves the best performance on seven of eight evaluated metrics. On GoogleEarth, our method achieves 75.56% spatial reasoning accuracy and 82.34% comparison accuracy, surpassing GeoProg3D by 11.56 and 22.61 percentage points, respectively. It also achieves lower counting and height estimation errors of 1.67 and 40.38 m, while remaining competitive in distance estimation. On UrbanScene3D, our method outperforms all compared approaches across all three metrics, achieving 68.33% spatial reasoning accuracy, 0.50 counting MAE, and 135.67 distance MAE. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of 3D CoCa v3 in both relational and metric spatial reasoning. Table 2. Comparison on City-3DQA [34]. Ablation Study Effect of contrastive learning objectives. Tab. 4 investigates the contributions of view-level and scene-level alignment during contrastive pre-training. Removing viewlevel alignment decreases overall Acc@1 from 64.79% to 62.05%, while removing scene-level alignment results in drop of 1.37 percentage points. Both variants exhibit degraded performance on multi-hop questions, with accuracy decreasing by 2.78 and 1.74 percentage points, respectively. These results highlight the complementary roles of finegrained view-level alignment and holistic scene-level alignment in learning geometry-aware representations for urban spatial reasoning. Table 4. Tab. 7 compares different strategies for incorporating scene captions into question answering. Sequential and alternating training achieve overall Acc@1 ranging from 62.59% to 63.20%. In contrast, integrating question-relevant captions achieves the highest overall Acc@1 of 64.79%, outperforming the strongest alternative by 1.59 percentage points. It also yields the best single-hop and multi-hop accuracies of 77.38% and 55.02%, respectively. These results suggest that question-guided caption retrieval provides complementary semantic and relational context for urban 3D spatial reasoning. Further ablations on decoder architectures and pretraining configurations are provided in the Supp. 5.5. Qualitative Analysis Fig. 4 presents qualitative comparisons on City-3DQA under the city-wise split. Our method correctly answers all four illustrated questions, highlighting its effectiveness in geometric understanding and relational reasoning in unseen urban scenes. Additional qualitative results are provided in the Supp. 6. Conclusion In this paper, we presented 3D CoCa v3, contrastive and generative framework for urban 3D scene understanding. Our framework employs an enhanced vision-language architecture with multi-scale geometric representations and language-model-based decoding. We further introduced MSG-based contrastive learning to incorporate structured spatial relationships into 3D-language representations, together with City3D-9.6K, multi-view urban dataset providing aligned visual-geometric observations and hierarchical language annotations. Extensive experiments on City-3DQA demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach, achieving 88.35% and 64.79% overall top-1 accuracy on the sentence-wise and city-wise splits, outperforming 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points, respectively. Moreover, 3D CoCa v3 achieved the best performance on GeoEval3D. These results highlight the effectiveness of jointly modeling geometric structures and relational semantics for urban 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning.

Additional Implementation Details We provide additional implementation details to facilitate reproducibility. Both training stages are conducted on four NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 80 GB memory each. The contrastive pre-training stage uses batch size of 32 and runs for 6,000 epochs, while the multimodal decoder stage uses batch size of 64. During pre-training, 32 multi-view observations are sampled per scene, with RGB images and corresponding point maps resized to 224 224. For downstream question answering, visual representations from 32 rendered views are extracted. For the decoder, we use 2B-parameter Qwen backbone with LoRA adaptation (rank 16 and α = 32) and an eight-head visual cross-attention module. The pretrained language-model parameters remain frozen, while the LoRA parameters, visual projection layers, and cross-attention module are optimized. C. Training Dynamics We provide the training loss curves of both stages to illustrate the optimization behavior of 3D CoCa v3. Fig. S1 illustrates the optimization dynamics of the contrastive pre-training stage. The overall objective and its individual components exhibit consistent decreasing trends throughout training. Although transient fluctuations are observed during optimization, the moving-average curves gradually stabilize, indicating stable convergence of the geometric, grounding, and cross-modal alignment objectives. Fig. S2 shows the training dynamics of the decoder stage over 15 epochs. The training loss decreases rapidly during the initial updates, followed by gradual reduction and stabilization in subsequent epochs. The moving-average curve Figure S1. Training curves of the contrastive pre-training stage. The top panel shows the overall pre-training objective Lpre = Lalign + Lground + Lgeo, while the remaining panels show the individual loss components. Light and dark curves represent per-epoch values and 101-epoch moving averages, respectively. All losses are plotted on logarithmic scale. and epoch-level means exhibit consistent trends despite perbatch fluctuations, suggesting stable optimization of the decoder. Figure S2. Training loss of the decoder stage. We report the perbatch training loss, its 101-step moving average, and the epochlevel mean over 15 training epochs. The loss decreases rapidly during the initial optimization stage and gradually stabilizes in subsequent epochs. D. Additional Qualitative Results Figs. S3 and S4 present additional qualitative comparisons on City-3DQA under the city-wise and sentence-wise splits, respectively. The examples cover object counting, functional relationships, and relative spatial reasoning using multi-view geometric and visual observations. 3D CoCa v3 correctly answers all illustrated questions in both splits, while competing methods exhibit errors in several counting and relational reasoning tasks. These results further illustrate the effectiveness of integrating multi-view geometric representations and structured relational information for urban 3D scene understanding. Figs. S5S8 present additional predictions across diverse urban scenes. The examples cover functional object counting, facility identification, relative spatial relationships, and accessibility reasoning, involving both singlehop and multi-hop questions. 3D CoCa v3 consistently produces predictions that match the ground-truth answers, including questions requiring fine-grained spatial localizaFigure S3. Additional qualitative comparisons on City-3DQA under the city-wise split. We compare 3D CoCa v3 with representative baselines on multi-hop and single-hop questions using multi-view RGB observations, point clouds, and corresponding XYZ point maps. Green checkmarks and red crosses indicate correct and incorrect predictions, respectively. Ground-truth (GT) answers are provided for reference. Figure S4. Additional qualitative comparisons on City-3DQA under the sentence-wise split. The examples focus on multi-hop questions involving object counting, functional relationships, and spatial reasoning. We compare predictions from different methods against the ground-truth (GT) answers. Green checkmarks and red crosses indicate correct and incorrect predictions, respectively. tion and reasoning over multiple urban functional regions. These results further demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in integrating multi-view geometric observations and structured spatial information for urban scene understanding. E. Limiation and Future Work Despite the promising results, 3D CoCa v3 has several limitations. First, our framework primarily focuses on static urban scene understanding and does not explicitly model temporal dynamics, such as moving objects and evolving spatial relationships. Second, although City3D-9.6K provides complementary multi-view geometric and relational supervision, its scene coverage remains limited compared with the diversity of real-world urban environments. Finally, while our method achieves strong performance in spatial reasoning and geometric understanding, fine-grained metric estimation and answer ranking still leave room for improvement. Future work will explore extending 3D CoCa v3 to dynamic urban environments by incorporating temporal representations and spatiotemporal relational reasoning. Figure S5. Additional qualitative results on urban functional understanding. Examples illustrate multi-hop and single-hop questions involving functional object counting, including educational, retail, residential, cultural, and governmental facilities. The predictions of 3D CoCa v3 consistently match the ground-truth (GT) answers. Figure S6. Additional qualitative results on urban spatial relationships. Examples demonstrate multi-hop reasoning about relative accessibility and spatial relationships among administrative, commercial, and residential areas, together with localized object counting and facility identification. 3D CoCa v3 correctly answers all illustrated questions. Figure S7. Additional qualitative results on fine-grained spatial reasoning. Examples involve spatially localized object counting, relative distance comparison, and facility existence in urban scenes containing office spaces and temporary structures. All predictions of 3D CoCa v3 are consistent with the ground-truth answers. Figure S8. Additional qualitative results on urban relational reasoning. Examples illustrate relative accessibility, spatial proximity, object counting, and facility existence involving marketplaces, public administration buildings, and commercial areas. 3D CoCa v3 correctly answers all illustrated single-hop and multi-hop questions.
